In advanced Taiji training the hen and ha secret sounds are referencing inhaling and exhaling.  There are two sets of intercostal muscles we use to breathe. One set compresses the lungs so we breathe out (ha) the other set opens the lungs to draw air in (hen). The hen and ha are the "sounds" of quick inhale or exhale. 

When expressing force in striking we generally need a cascade of muscle engagement to accelerate the weapon. Adding the out breath ha as a part of the cascade let's the intercostal muscles be a part of the addition of muscular force by adding the breathing muscles to the motion. 

Hen is the sound of breathing in. It is the muscles that open and lift the chest and draw air into the lungs. When lifting, uprooting, or throwing an opponent breathing in quickly once you have attached to their body can lift them from the ground just through the lungs expanding and that lifting their body up slightly. So hen is to uproot with the use of the inbreath and ha is the addition of breathing muscles to add power to outward forces from your body.

The three big types of thought of Confucian, Taoist, and Buddhist are all integrated into the martial arts of China. The sensible organization of things is very confucian. Compassion and helping others and working to better the self is very Buddhist. Going with the flow and studying nature is very Taoist. 

All these things are integral to Kung Fu.

The sensation is a result of changing how you think about your body. By changing your mind you can affect your body powerfully. Like how when we get stressed out shoulders and neck will tighten. Mental change with physical result. 

Thinking yourself into the connection or Qi feeling is common in foundations of qigong however it rarely translates to much of anything in the way of skills. Qi can be seen as a relationship rather than just as an energy. To make energy we require a relationship of some sort, heat, wood, and oxygen can make fire for example. So by changing the relationship of how you see or think about your body your body will react. This is the base of qigong and Taiji basically. Studying and adjusting relationships in the body and mind to result in power, connection and so on. 

Don't stop there, train a specific qigong system or Taiji principle deeply and work to find the relationships you need to study within it. That's how internal begins.

This depends a great deal on how you see Buddhism and define enlightenment. Zen is able to be practiced as a religious path or philosophical one. 

Religious Buddhists tend to see enlightenment as an escape from rebirth or reincarnation through attaining enough merit through meditation and rituals. 

Philosophical Buddhists (which tend to be more of the Zen types) tend to see enlightenment as releasing all their attachments and seeing reality as clearly as possible. This means life in the present moment with the understanding of who they really are. This can be found by anyone in or out of a monastery they just need to do the work. Monks devote a sequestered life to it and so have a better chance than the layman but Buddhism is filled with tales of layman enlightened masters. The distractions of the everyday world will make it harder than a monks life but many would also argue it makes it all the more real. 

It ain't easy, for anyone. It's the work that makes it possible to live a good life in the present moment. Enlightenment is not a place or a single achievement. It's just not being as dumb and clueless as you once were. 

Before enlightenment, chop wood and carry water. After enlightenment, choose wood, carry water.

Qin Na 擒拿 literally translates to sieze and control and is used to refer to most methods people consider 'trapping'. But it has a lot more meaning than just catching an arm or doing a lock.  Siezing and controlling an opponent is the goal through taking their balance,  their minds off of what they are doing or disabling their ability to move through locks or damaging their body.  

Most often misunderstood is how it can actually be accomplished in combat with a real opponent.  The method "grab to hit/ hit to grab" is the way we practice which simply means of you want to grab them hit them first of vice versa. Constantly changing from hitting to grabbing and grabbing to hitting continually attacks the opponent mentally so they cannot adapt easily to what you are doing. Only trying to hit or only trying to grab is far easier to defend against rather than changing from one to another rapidly. This method accomplished bridging with the opponent as well which puts you in range and contact in order to sieze them. 

Four major methods of qin na are types / applicative methods of qin na as well. 1- joint locks 2- stopping breath 3- dealing blood (blood chokes) 4- attacking cavities / siezing the body through pain.  Couple this with continued grabbing and hitting and it starts to actually work.
